name: Autumn Oak
lede: Autumn Oak is a dark reddish brown first dated by Maerz and Paul to 1927, close to Mahogany but a little warmer.

sections.title: A 1927 landscape word
sections.body: ColorHub's library traces Autumn Oak to Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, which puts its first record in 1927 and locates it on plate 7, swatch H9 [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system, which cites the same dictionary, classes it as a grayish reddish brown [1]. It is built on a season and a tree, not a dye or pigment: our tagging calls it a landscape word rather than a material [1]. The nearest named colors on file are [[bole]] and [[tuscan-red]], at Both sit in and [[carbuncle]], two names that keep it company on canvas more often than chance [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a close match to Autumn Oak in 440 of 23,781 paintings (1.85 percent), as photographed, with the stricter within-painting reading at 232 [2]. It is more common than 73 percent of our named colors [2]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 21 of 945 paintings, at twice the archive's overall rate for that century [2].

Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, by lightness rank, so varnish and glare cannot fake the finding [2]. The earliest dated match in the archive is from 1100, eight centuries before the name itself was recorded, which only shows a similar hue was photographed there, not that anyone called it Autumn Oak, or used a matching pigment, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].

origin.first_recorded: Maerz and Paul, 1930 (plate 7, swatch H9; first recorded 1927)
